package_info.package_manager: Windows PE (standalone binary, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: Azov is a destructive wiper malware designed to irreversibly corrupt user data and backdoor legitimate executables for persistence. It employs advanced anti-analysis and polymorphic techniques, with no monetization or recovery intent, making its sole purpose sabotage and destruction.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the Azov binary is executed)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: For each targeted file: Overwrite 666 bytes, skip 666 bytes, repeat this pattern up to 4GB per file.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code iterates over files and overwrites 666 bytes, skips 666 bytes, and repeats this alternating pattern up to 4GB, resulting in partial but unrecoverable file corruption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Selective, patterned overwriting of file contents is a hallmark of wiper malware, designed to maximize destruction while optimizing speed.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not irreversibly corrupt user files in a patterned, non-recoverable way.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Secure file deletion utilities may overwrite files, but typically with user consent and not in a partial, alternating pattern.
key_indicators: No attempt at recovery or user notification

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after initial execution, during infection spread)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Inject polymorphic, modified Azov code into legitimate EXE files on the system.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code locates legitimate EXE files and injects a polymorphic, backdoored version of itself into them, ensuring persistence and further spread upon execution of those files.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-injection into unrelated executables is a classic malware persistence and propagation technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate programs should not modify or backdoor other executables on the system.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate patchers or updaters may modify executables, but not to inject self-replicating, destructive code.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Implements anti-analysis: opaque predicates, anti-debug, syntactic bloat, junk code, CALL instead of RET/JMP, dynamic Import Address Table creation.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code employs multiple anti-analysis techniques to evade detection and hinder reverse engineering, including opaque predicates, anti-debugging, syntactic bloat, and dynamic API resolution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of multiple anti-analysis and obfuscation techniques is typical of sophisticated malware aiming to evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely employs such extensive anti-analysis measures, especially in destructive utilities.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some commercial software uses anti-debugging to protect intellectual property, but not in destructive tools.

attack_chain.action: Initial execution of the Azov wiper binary on the victim system.
attack_chain.leads_to: File destruction and persistence mechanisms are triggered.

attack_chain.action: Destructive wiping of user files using the 666-byte alternating overwrite pattern.
Polymorphic injection of Azov code into legitimate EXE files for persistence and further spread.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ensures malware persists and re-executes when infected EXEs are run.

attack_chain.action: Anti-analysis and evasion techniques are employed to hinder detection and analysis.
attack_chain.leads_to: Increases difficulty of detection and reverse engineering, prolonging the attack window.

behavioral_signatures: Alternating overwrite/skip patterns in file writes (e.g., 666 bytes overwritten, 666 bytes skipped)
Injection of polymorphic code into unrelated EXE files
Extensive use of anti-debugging and anti-analysis techniques in binaries
file_indicators: Legitimate EXE files with appended or injected code sections
Files partially overwritten in a repeating pattern (e.g., 666 bytes on/off)
Presence of binaries with FASM-compiled assembly code and obfuscation
network_indicators: None observed for Azov (no C2 or exfiltration in described version)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unusual file write patterns, especially partial overwrites in a repeating pattern (e.g., 666 bytes on/off). Detect modifications to legitimate EXE files, particularly those with new or suspicious code sections. Use behavioral analysis to flag binaries employing multiple anti-analysis techniques. Hash-based detection for known Azov samples (e.g., 650f0d694c0928d88aeeed649cf629fc8a7bec604563bca716b1688227e0cc7e) and YARA rules for FASM-compiled, obfuscated assembly code are recommended.
